title: The First Message Ever Sent on the Internet Crashed After Two Letters
description: On October 29, 1969, a UCLA student tried to type one word to a computer 350 miles away. The system crashed after two letters. This is the story of how that fragile experiment became the internet, and why nobody planned for what it became.
notes: FACT-CHECK before recording: Oct 29, 1969 about 10:30 pm, UCLA (Charley Kline, Leonard Kleinrock's lab) to SRI (Bill Duvall), ~350 miles; the L-O-G exchange over the phone and the crash on G; fix and success about an hour later; Kleinrock's 'Lo and behold' remark (paraphrase); Bob Taylor's three terminals (1966) and the ~$1 million approved in ~20 minutes (Herzfeld, reported); nuclear-war myth (ARPANET's goal was resource sharing); Baran/Davies packet switching and AT&T skepticism (reported); BBN IMPs (refrigerator-sized); four nodes Dec 1969 (UCLA, SRI, UCSB, Utah); Tomlinson's @ email 1971 and share of traffic by 1973 (hedge); Cerf and Kahn TCP/IP; Jan 1, 1983 switch; Berners-Lee 1989 proposal and 'vague but exciting' note; first website 1991; CERN royalty-free 1993; 'more than five billion people online'. Distinguish the internet (network) from the web (service). Target runtime ~8+ min (check real audio length).

scenes.text: At about ten-thirty on the night of October twenty-ninth, nineteen sixty-nine, a graduate student at UCLA sat down at a computer terminal and began to type one word: L-O-G-I-N. At the other end of the line, three hundred and fifty miles away at the Stanford Research Institute, a researcher held a telephone to his ear. "Did you get the L?" "Got the L." "Did you get the O?" "Got the O." "Did you get the G?" And then, silence. The computer had crashed.
scenes.image: UCLA Boelter Hall room 3420 ARPANET plaque
scenes.visual: a dark lab; a terminal; letters typing L, O, then a glitch; a phone call bubble; a map line between Los Angeles and Stanford with "~350 miles".

scenes.text: That crash, two letters into the very first message, is the birth of the internet. And the strangest part of this story is that almost nobody who built it imagined what it would become.
scenes.visual: two letters glowing, then a network of lines spreading outward from them.

scenes.text: To understand how they got there, go back to nineteen sixty-six, to a government office at the Pentagon. A man named Bob Taylor ran a research program for the military's advanced research agency. In his office sat three computer terminals. Each was connected to a different computer, in a different city. And each spoke a different language.
scenes.visual: an office with three terminals, each labelled with a different city and a different command style.

scenes.text: To talk to all three, Taylor had to switch chairs, log in separately, and remember three sets of commands. It struck him as ridiculous. Why shouldn't all these machines be able to talk to each other? Reportedly, he pitched the idea to his boss, and had about a million dollars approved in twenty minutes.
scenes.visual: a man swivelling between three chairs; the three terminals joined by one glowing line; a stopwatch showing 20 minutes and a $1M tag.

scenes.text: You'll often hear that the internet was built to survive a nuclear war. It's a popular story. But the people who built the network say that wasn't the goal. The goal was much simpler: expensive computers were scattered across the country, and researchers wanted to share them.
scenes.visual: a mushroom cloud icon crossed out; scattered computers on a map linked by lines; the words "sharing, not survival".

scenes.text: The big technical idea was something called packet switching. Instead of holding a line open, like a phone call, you break a message into small pieces, called packets. Each one finds its own way across the network, and they're put back together at the other end. Imagine mailing a book by tearing it into postcards.
scenes.visual: a book tearing into postcards; each taking a different route across a map; reassembling into the book.

scenes.text: The idea came from more than one place. Paul Baran in the United States and Donald Davies in Britain both worked it out, independently. And the giant telephone company of the time, AT&T, reportedly told Baran it would never work. Phone lines, they said, were meant for calls.
scenes.image: Paul Baran Donald Davies packet switching
scenes.visual: two name cards (Baran, Davies) with flags; a phone company logo with a "won't work" stamp.

scenes.text: A small Boston firm, Bolt Beranek and Newman, won the contract to build the machines that would sit at each site. Called Interface Message Processors, each was about the size of a refrigerator. Their job was to be the middlemen, receiving packets and passing them along.
scenes.visual: a refrigerator-sized machine labelled "IMP" with arrows entering and leaving; a small BBN tag.

scenes.text: The first one arrived at UCLA in the autumn of nineteen sixty-nine, in the lab of a professor named Leonard Kleinrock. The second went to the Stanford Research Institute. Two machines, three hundred and fifty miles apart, joined by a leased telephone line. And a graduate student named Charley Kline, with a very short message to send.
scenes.visual: an IMP arriving in a lab; a leased line stretching up the coast; Kleinrock's and Kline's name cards.

scenes.text: After the crash, the team found the bug and fixed it. About an hour later, they tried again. This time, the whole word went through: L-O-G-I-N. The first message had failed. The second succeeded. And the network was alive.
scenes.visual: a retry button; a progress bar; the full word LOGIN typing out; a green check.

scenes.text: Years later, Kleinrock pointed out something that made people smile. Those first two letters, L and O, could be read as the beginning of a phrase: lo and behold. By accident, the very first message on the internet was a kind of announcement. Short. Fragile. And somehow, exactly right.
scenes.visual: the letters L-O bursting into "Lo and behold"; a faint smile from a lab figure.

scenes.text: By December of nineteen sixty-nine, the network had four computers. UCLA. The Stanford Research Institute. UC Santa Barbara. And the University of Utah. Four machines in four labs. That was the entire internet.
scenes.visual: a map of the western United States with four glowing dots connecting one by one.

scenes.text: Then something happened that nobody had planned. In nineteen seventy-one, an engineer named Ray Tomlinson sent a message from one computer to another, and picked a symbol to separate the user's name from the machine's name. The at sign. He had just invented email.
scenes.visual: a name, then an "@" popping in, then a machine name; an envelope icon flying between two computers.

scenes.text: Within a few years, email was most of the traffic on the network. The designers had built a system for sharing expensive computers. What people actually wanted was to talk to each other. It's a pattern that would repeat again and again in the story of the internet.
scenes.visual: a traffic bar: "computing" tiny, "email" huge; people icons chatting across the network.

scenes.text: But there was a new problem. Other networks were being built, and they couldn't talk to each other. In the mid-nineteen-seventies, two engineers, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, designed a common language that every network could speak. It was called TCP/IP. Think of it as a shared grammar for machines.
scenes.image: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn TCP/IP
scenes.visual: several separate networks with different shapes; a common language layer sliding over them; two name cards (Cerf, Kahn).

scenes.text: On January first, nineteen eighty-three, the old ARPANET switched over to TCP/IP. Many people call that day the true birth of the internet: not one network, but a network of networks, all speaking the same language.
scenes.visual: a calendar flipping to January 1; networks snapping together into a mesh of networks.

scenes.text: And still, the internet wasn't something most people could use. It was a road, without any shops. Then, in nineteen eighty-nine, a British scientist at the European research lab CERN, Tim Berners-Lee, proposed a way to link documents together. His boss, according to the story, wrote on the proposal: vague, but exciting.
scenes.visual: a road labelled "internet"; a proposal page with a handwritten note; linked documents appearing on the road.

scenes.text: That idea became the World Wide Web. The first website went online in nineteen ninety-one. And in nineteen ninety-three, CERN made the technology free for anyone to use. That's the difference. The internet is the network. The web is something you use on it. One is the road. The other is the places you can go.
scenes.visual: a road and a map of destinations; a "royalty-free" stamp; a browser window opening.

scenes.text: Today, more than five billion people are online. They send messages to each other every second, in every language, across every ocean. All of it descends from a single fragile experiment, in which a student typed one word, and the machine died after two letters.
scenes.visual: a world map lighting up with connections; a counter rising past five billion; two letters in the corner.

scenes.text: And here's what makes the story so human. The people who built it were not trying to change the world. They were trying to solve a tiny problem: three terminals, three languages, one frustrated man. The first message failed. They fixed it, and they tried again.
scenes.visual: Taylor's three terminals returning; a retry arrow; "fix, then try again" in large type.

scenes.text: Remember those two letters. L. O. A crash, and a promise. The best inventions rarely announce themselves with a bang. They begin as something small, and a little broken. Which is exactly why so many people miss them.
scenes.visual: the opening dark lab; the letters L and O glowing in the dark.

scenes.text: Next time: two students tried to sell their idea for one million dollars. The buyer said no. That idea became Google.
scenes.visual: two student silhouettes holding a paper; a "$1M" tag; a buyer waving no; end card: channel name.
